Testing sends you back to redesign, feedback back to the specification, and a product in production feeds into the next model.
A short statement of what is to be designed, for whom and why, agreed between designer and client.
A detailed list of measurable criteria the design must meet, written from research — e.g. 'must weigh under 500 g'.
Putting the needs, wants and abilities of the end user at the centre of every decision, involving them throughout.
An accurate, dimensioned technical drawing with all the information needed to make a product — sizes, tolerances, materials and finishes.
Tells the factory exactly how to make the product — materials, processes, machine settings, assembly sequence, tolerances and finishes.
Quality control checks and tests products to find faults; quality assurance designs the process so faults are less likely in the first place.
Designing products, systems and environments to fit the people who use them, so they are comfortable, safe and efficient.
The collection and use of human body measurement data to make ergonomic decisions.

front: Why design for the 5th to 95th percentile?
back: It covers most of the population — a product designed only for the average fits almost nobody exactly.
Designing by imitating forms, processes and systems in nature — e.g. Velcro (burrs), honeycomb panels, shark-skin swimwear, kingfisher-beak train noses.
